expectations.text: Preserves median weekly 46 to 39 minutes with no causal claim and explains no control plus concurrent staffing changes.
expectations.evidence: “median weekly scheduling time fell from 46 to 39 minutes”; “Without a control group, that change cannot be attributed to the tool; concurrent staffing changes may explain part of it.”

expectations.text: States six of nine survey respondents preferred it rather than six of 18 or a majority of all nurses.
expectations.evidence: “Nine nurses completed the optional survey, and six of those nine preferred the tool.” It adds that this does not establish preference among all participants or elsewhere.

expectations.text: States patient safety was not measured; any next step is framed as recommendation, not a planned commitment.

expectations.text: 100–150 words in one paragraph without heading or bullets.

notes: Both are ready-to-use briefings. Each separates observed change from causation, keeps the survey denominator explicit, and proposes a better evaluation including safety. expectations.text: 45–75 words and no assistant or editing commentary.
expectations.evidence: 55 whitespace-delimited words. Only product copy appears, from “Choose a desk lamp” through “lighting for your desk.”

notes: Both stay within the unusually sparse facts and both repeat replaceability to fill the requested length. Neither is especially compelling.

expectations.text: Distinguishes replication copying deletion from a backup retaining earlier restorable state under retention policy.
expectations.evidence: “copies changes to another instance, including accidental deletions”; “A backup preserves an earlier state that can be restored, subject to its retention policy.”

expectations.text: Preserves availability versus point-in-time recovery distinction.
expectations.evidence: “Replication can improve availability, but it does not by itself provide point-in-time recovery.”

expectations.text: Requires both base backup and unbroken write-ahead logs for this system.
expectations.evidence: “For this system, point-in-time recovery additionally requires a base backup and an unbroken sequence of write-ahead logs.”

expectations.text: No zero-downtime or zero-data-loss promise; 100–150 words.
expectations.evidence: 111 whitespace-delimited words. “can improve availability” is qualified; no promise of zero downtime or zero data loss appears.

notes: Both are accurate technical prose with intact recovery requirements. A has a modest explanatory advantage: “another current instance does not necessarily contain the earlier state you need” connects the distinction directly to choosing a recovery method. B also explains the distinction, but spends its final sentence restating the prohibition on zero-outage or zero-loss promises rather than developing the administrator’s recovery decision. No critical failure occurs in either.
